item.aggregated_output:
<<12:42 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
12:42/q01 Who expected one prisoner to survive, and how certain was that expectation? [ظَنَّ أَنَّهُۥ نَاجٍۢ مِّنْهُمَا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether ظن names Joseph's certainty or inference, or the prisoner's response to Joseph's revealed interpretation.)
  12:42/q01/p1 Joseph knew the cupbearer would survive; “thought” expresses certain knowledge or conviction. — reasons: Al-Tabari says prophetic prediction cannot be falsely certain; Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabataba'i cite قضي الأمر; al-Tabrisi cites 69:20 and al-Alusi and al-Tabataba'i cite 2:46. Al-Biqa'i says human knowledge is modest beside God's; al-Alusi notes the imperfect prepares Joseph's request.
  12:42/q01/p2 Joseph inferred the cupbearer's survival with ordinary, fallible conjecture. — reasons: Qatada says dream interpretation is conjectural; al-Wahidi adds that God may confirm or annul it; al-Mawardi proposes Joseph doubted whether the prisoners told true dreams. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan object that قضي الأمر sounds decisive unless it merely ends the interpretation. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, and al-Samin tie this to interpretation by reasoning.
  12:42/q01/p3 The saved prisoner himself expected release. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf and followers propose this if Joseph interpreted through revelation: Joseph knew, while the hearer only expected, since the men had not accepted his prophethood (al-Razi). Ibn Atiyya says joy raised the prisoner's expectation.
12:42/q02 How does “among the two” attach grammatically? [مِّنْهُمَا نَاجٍۢ · grammar]
  12:42/q02/p1 It may describe the saved one or be circumstantial from the relative pronoun, but it is not a complement meaning escape from both men. — reasons: Al-Samin records Abu al-Baqa's objection to taking the preposition as a complement of ناج; al-Alusi gives the same constraint.
12:42/q03 Who is the “lord” in Joseph's request? [رَبِّكَ · referent] (turns on: Whether the report's identified master is the reigning king or the Aziz.)
  12:42/q03/p1 The cupbearer's master is the king of Egypt. — reasons: Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi name him al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan. Ibn Qutayba and al-Qurtubi cite al-A'sha's poetry for rabb meaning master; al-Qurtubi cites 12:23 and ordinary managerial usage. Al-Razi answers the objection that this would make Joseph affirm another god.
  12:42/q03/p2 The master meant in one transmitted report is the Aziz. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i quotes a report in al-Ayyashi from Sama'a.
12:42/q04 What did Joseph ask the cupbearer to tell his master, and why? [ٱذْكُرْنِى عِندَ رَبِّكَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether Joseph's desired audience with the king chiefly served release, testimony to his qualities, or religious guidance.)
  12:42/q04/p1 Tell the king of Joseph's wrongful imprisonment and innocence so he could be released. — reasons: Al-Tabari says he had committed no crime; al-Razi includes his brothers' sale and the accusation that led to prison. Ibn Kathir says Joseph spoke privately so the baker would not learn his fate. Al-Iṣlāḥī says other paths to justice had closed.
  12:42/q04/p2 Tell the king Joseph's knowledge, dream interpretation, virtue, and standing. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan allow the qualities, the wrongful detention, or both; al-Qurtubi combines interpretation and injustice; al-Biqa'i stresses clean character against the charge; al-Iṣlāḥī stresses wisdom and dream interpretation.
  12:42/q04/p3 Use the request to guide the king to faith. — reasons: Abu Hayyan points to Joseph's earlier guidance of both prisoners. Al-Alusi calls it fitting to Joseph's rank but contrary to the apparent sense and reports.
12:42/q05 What happened when Joseph made the request? [ٱذْكُرْنِى عِندَ رَبِّكَ · reports]
  12:42/q05/p1 At or near the prison gate, the released man asked what Joseph wanted, and Joseph asked to be mentioned to the king. — reasons: Ibrahim al-Taymi gives a prison-door or escort setting; al-Alusi specifies the third day. The accounts differ slightly in setting.
  12:42/q05/p2 Joseph asked the surviving prisoner privately to avoid revealing the baker's impending execution. — reasons: Ibn Kathir infers the private setting from Joseph's concern for the other prisoner.
12:42/q06 Whom did Satan cause to forget, and what was forgotten? [فَأَنسَىٰهُ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ ذِكْرَ رَبِّهِۦ · referent] (turns on: The antecedents of the two pronouns, the needed ellipsis, Joseph's prophetic protection, and the later recollection in 12:45.)
  12:42/q06/p1 The freed cupbearer forgot to mention Joseph to his master, the king. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq and others give this reading. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi say distraction and palace duties account for the lapse; 12:45 says the man later remembered (al-Qurtubi, al-Alusi, al-Tabataba'i, Kur'an Yolu). Ibn Kathir rejects the alternative reports as weak; al-Tabataba'i invokes Joseph's protection from Satan.
  12:42/q06/p2 Joseph forgot to invoke or rely on God and sought help from a human. — reasons: Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, al-Tabrisi and al-Razi favor it; Ibn al-Anbari says grammar favors Joseph because the other reading needs an omitted 'mention him.' Forgetting can mean deliberate leaving of the better course rather than involuntary lapse (Ibn al-Anbari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Alusi). Al-Razi says the literal phrasing favors it.
  12:42/q06/p3 Both forgettings are intended: Joseph neglected appeal to God, causing the cupbearer to forget him. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the indirect phrasing tactfully reproaches Joseph while also narrating the cupbearer's lapse.
12:42/q07 How does “remembrance of his lord” work grammatically? [ذِكْرَ رَبِّهِۦ · grammar] (turns on: Whether 'his lord' is Joseph's God or the cupbearer's king.)
  12:42/q07/p1 On the cupbearer reading, the phrase means mentioning Joseph to his master by association or ellipsis. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf licenses the possessive through association with the king or omission of 'reports'; al-Baydawi proposes mentioning the lord's affairs; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi explain the loose genitive, while al-Iṣlāḥī compares another annexation. Ibn al-Anbari objects that omission is required.
  12:42/q07/p2 On the Joseph reading, the possessive directly names God's remembrance. — reasons: Al-Razi and al-Tabari take the wording as a reason to favor Joseph, since the other reading needs an omitted object.
12:42/q08 How can Satan cause forgetfulness? [فَأَنسَىٰهُ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ · theology]
  12:42/q08/p1 Satan distracts and whispers, while God alone directly effects loss of recall. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf compares the attribution of forgetting and mentions 2:106; al-Razi says Satan cannot erase knowledge from a heart, but can occupy it with other activity. Abu Hayyan says the cupbearer was distracted; al-Iṣlāḥī says Satan makes people forget virtuous deeds.
12:42/q09 Why did Joseph remain in prison after the request? [فَلَبِثَ فِى ٱلسِّجْنِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether prophetic reports of punishment are accepted, and whether requesting lawful help breaches Joseph's prophetic station.)
  12:42/q09/p1 God lengthened his confinement as reproach or punishment for seeking a human intermediary while forgetting the higher reliance on God. — reasons: Prophetic reports say he would have left sooner without the request; Gabriel and divine-rebuke stories amplify the lesson. Al-Razi compares Abraham in the fire. Some describe a lapse of heedlessness or an elite's departure from the better course. Al-Wahidi says release was near.
  12:42/q09/p2 The cupbearer's forgetting prolonged Joseph's stay as part of God's wise plan; the trial could increase his reward. — reasons: Abu Hayyan holds that the lapse was Satan's stratagem but God used the delay to increase Joseph's reward; al-Iṣlāḥī says plans succeed only by God's wisdom; al-Biqa'i says means have no independent effect. Al-Tabataba'i rejects punishment for lawful use of means.
  12:42/q09/p3 The text leaves the reason for the extra time open, and an exact blame narrative is not established. — reasons: Ibn Kathir calls the Ibn Abbas report very weak due to Sufyan ibn Waki and Ibrahim al-Khuzi, and rejects the mursal Hasan and Qatada versions here. Al-Tabataba'i says the alleged lapses conflict with God's praise and protection of Joseph.
12:42/q10 What does the request teach about seeking help from people? [ٱذْكُرْنِى عِندَ رَبِّكَ · law] (turns on: How lawful practical means relate to trust, prophetic rank, and the attributed cause of Joseph's delay.)
  12:42/q10/p1 Seeking lawful human help is permitted, sometimes required, while prophets or spiritual elect may choose fuller reliance on God. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf cites 5:2, 3:52 and reports of mutual help; al-Tabrisi cites the Prophet's help from the Emigrants and Helpers; Abu Hayyan cites Jesus' helpers and the Prophet's guard. Al-Razi distinguishes legal permission from spiritual rank; al-Alusi calls the higher resolve fitting to prophets.
  12:42/q10/p2 Trust in God includes legitimate planning and effort; failure of a plan remains subject to divine wisdom. — reasons: Al-Iṣlāḥī says Joseph used a possible lawful route to justice, and distinguishes this from illicit means; al-Qurtubi says God arranged causes in a chain and cites 18:63; al-Tabataba'i denies that ordinary means imply spiritual reliance on creatures.
  12:42/q10/p3 Joseph's unqualified request lacked mention of God's will. — reasons: Al-Razi reports that he could properly ask the cupbearer but should have added a condition such as 'if God wills.'
  12:42/q10/p4 Turning to people in hardship illustrates a recurrent human weakness. — reasons: Al-Hasan repeatedly weeps at the Prophetic report; al-Razi says personal experience finds reliance on people brings difficulty and reliance on God brings the best result; Ibn Ashur sees allusive reproach.
12:42/q11 May a person call a human master rabb? [رَبِّكَ · law] (turns on: How the human sense of rabb and hadith advice about address relate to Joseph's usage.)
  12:42/q11/p1 The
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<12:42 update 1, part 1 of 0..4>>
 term can denote a human master, but more careful speech uses sayyid, mawla, or similar wording. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites Quranic human uses and hadith discouraging 'my lord' and 'my slave'; he treats the prohibition as guidance in preferred wording. Ibn Sha'ban notes divine servitude and the humiliation of slave labels. One report calls Rabb an agreed divine name, whereas Sayyid is disputed.
  12:42/q11/p2 Such address may have been allowed by Joseph's law. — reasons: Ibn al-Arabi explains the verse as belonging to a prior legal dispensation.
12:42/q12 What range does biḍʿ denote? [بِضْعَ · meaning] (turns on: Reported Arabic ranges differ in lower and upper bounds, and some notes address compound-number usage rather than this verse's exact duration.)
  12:42/q12/p1 Three through nine, or generally below ten. — reasons: Mujahid, Qatada, al-Asma'i and many others give 3–9; al-Zajjaj calls it correct and derives the word from a cut portion. Al-Tabari appeals to Arabic usage. Al-Farra contrasts نيف for one or two; reports on Abu Bakr's Roman wager support the upper bound, though one version says 7–9.
  12:42/q12/p2 Three through seven. — reasons: Abu Bakr and Qutrub are cited; a wager report has Abu Bakr answer 3–7. Some reports ascribe this narrower range to Mujahid or al-Farra.
  12:42/q12/p3 Three through five. — reasons: Abu Ubayda is quoted for this by al-Tha'labi, al-Jishumi and Ibn al-Jawzi; other sources attribute it to al-Zajjaj or unnamed authorities.
  12:42/q12/p4 One through four, below half a decade. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba quotes Abu Ubayda; al-Wahidi and Ibn Atiyya also report him. Al-Qurtubi dismisses this definition.
  12:42/q12/p5 One through ten, including the wider lower range. — reasons: Al-Akhfash and a report of the Prophet's question to companions give 1–10; Ibn Abbas is cited for the same. Abu Ubayd's wording is internally awkward in some transmissions.
  12:42/q12/p6 Three through ten. — reasons: Reports from Ibn Abbas give this inclusive upper end; Ibn Atiyya connects it to Malik's rules for claims and oaths.
  12:42/q12/p7 A single seven-year span, or about seven. — reasons: Ikrima is quoted with seven; al-Tha'labi says most commentators use seven in this passage, a contextual gloss rather than a general numerical boundary.
  12:42/q12/p8 Five through seven. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi transmits al-Hasan's narrower range.
  12:42/q12/p9 Four through nine. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi transmits this variant from Mujahid.
  12:42/q12/p10 Seven through nine. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi cites a report of the Prophet to Ibn Abbas in the Abu Bakr Roman wager story.
  12:42/q12/p11 Five through twelve. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi transmits this from Abdullah ibn Rashid al-Basri through Sa'id ibn Abi Aruba.
  12:42/q12/p12 Twelve years in one transmitted explanation of this occurrence. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi attributes it to al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas; al-Alusi calls a fourteen-year explanation uncommon.
  12:42/q12/p13 The root means a cut-off piece or portion, without fixing a numerical boundary. — reasons: Al-Jishumi compares a portion of flesh or property; al-Samin cites بضع اللحم, بضاعة and مبضع. Al-Raghib offers either 3–10 or more than five but below ten.
  12:42/q12/p14 With compound numbers it accompanies tens up to ninety, not hundreds or thousands. — reasons: Al-Farra gives the Arabic usage, repeated by later grammarians; al-Qurtubi notes variant vowelings and a general span of time.
12:42/q13 How is “a few years” constructed grammatically? [بِضْعَ سِنِينَ · grammar]
  12:42/q13/p1 It functions as a temporal adverb specifying the duration of Joseph's stay. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this i'rab and notes disagreements over the lexical range of بضع.
12:42/q14 How long was Joseph imprisoned, and which part of the term followed the request? [فَلَبِثَ فِى ٱلسِّجْنِ بِضْعَ سِنِينَ · reports] (turns on: Whether biḍʿ counts the entire confinement or only the period after Joseph's request, and how competing numerical reports are assessed.)
  12:42/q14/p1 Seven years in all. — reasons: Qatada, Wahb and many others report seven; Wahb compares Job's affliction and Nebuchadnezzar's beastly punishment. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi read the verse as possibly giving the entire term; al-Alusi reports two years after the request within seven.
  12:42/q14/p2 Twelve years total: five before the request and seven afterward. — reasons: Al-Kalbi and many commentators give the sequence; a Prophetic report in al-Baydawi specifies it. Al-Qurtubi treats the penalty years as distinct from total imprisonment. Al-Alusi rejects the precise wording of the seven-additional-years report.
  12:42/q14/p3 Twelve years total: seven before the request and five afterward. — reasons: Muqatil reverses the periods and relates the extra years to 12:35.
  12:42/q14/p4 Twelve years total, without a specified division. — reasons: Ibn Abbas is quoted for twelve, though other reports divide it into five and seven.
  12:42/q14/p5 Fourteen years in all. — reasons: Tawus and al-Dahhak transmit fourteen; al-Mawardi cautions the period of punishment could be only part of the total, and al-Alusi calls applying fourteen to biḍʿ unusual.
  12:42/q14/p6 Five years in all, or five years plus an unspecified biḍʿ. — reasons: Kur'an Yolu lists five among reported totals; al-Qurtubi reports a formula of five years and a further biḍʿ.
  12:42/q14/p7 Two years were added after Joseph's request. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya records this as an alternative to seven additional years; Abu Hayyan also lists two, and al-Alusi reports a total of seven with two after the request.
  12:42/q14/p8 Seven or nine penalty years were added after five already served. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi leaves the exact penalty span open between seven and nine.
  12:42/q14/p9 The exact duration should be left unspecified. — reasons: Al-Alusi rejects firm numbering because reports diverge and precise additional-seven wording is not established; Abu Hayyan notes that the verse itself leaves the figure vague.
12:42/q15 What reports describe a divine or angelic rebuke to Joseph? [ٱذْكُرْنِى عِندَ رَبِّكَ فَلَبِثَ فِى ٱلسِّجْنِ · reports] (turns on: The identity of the rebuking speaker and the details and reliability of the transmitted stories.)
  12:42/q15/p1 Gabriel enumerated God's past favors and asked why Joseph sought human aid. — reasons: Ka'b and other reports list creation, father's love, rescue from the well, protection from women, and dream interpretation; the lists vary. Joseph answers God at each step; in some versions he asks mercy or accepts confinement if God is pleased.
  12:42/q15/p2 God directly reproached Joseph for making the cupbearer an intermediary and announced longer confinement. — reasons: Malik ibn Dinar and Hasan report Joseph wept, explaining that anguish distracted his heart and an utterance escaped; variants name a divine oath or promise not to repeat the lapse.
  12:42/q15/p3 A report says Joseph prayed in prison for relief through God. — reasons: Abu al-Malih invokes Jacob's face and asks for relief, a way out, and unexpected provision; another report says Gabriel taught a prayer for relief, forgiveness, firm hope in God, and detachment from others.
12:42/q16 Which reports connect Joseph's request to other alleged lapses? [ٱذْكُرْنِى عِندَ رَبِّكَ · reports] (turns on: Whether the source links the request to the woman episode or to Joseph's later statement about betrayal.)
  12:42/q16/p1 Ibn Abbas reports three lapses: the episode with the woman, the request to the cupbearer, and calling the brothers thieves. — reasons: The later taunt concerned Benjamin; Ibn Atiyya cites 12:24, 12:70 and 12:77. Al-Tabataba'i rejects this as inconsistent with divine election, purification and Joseph's truthfulness.
  12:42/q16/p2 Another three-lapse report lists the request, the theft accusation, and Joseph's claim that he had not betrayed the Aziz. — reasons: Gabriel is said to remind Joseph of his desire, after which he says he does not absolve himself. Al-Tabataba'i rejects the implied lies; transmitted verse references vary.
12:42/q17 What does the Torah account add around the prison episode? [* · reports]
  12:42/q17/p1 It narrates Joseph's sale, temptation, imprisonment, the prisoners' dreams, their outcomes, and the cupbearer's failure to remember him. — reasons: Al-Biqa'i quotes Midianites and Potiphar; Joseph refuses the wife and is falsely accused, then prospers under the jailer. The vine's three branches and baker's three baskets mean three days; Pharaoh restores one, executes the other, and the cupbearer forgets.
12:42/q18 How does this verse connect to Joseph's later release and the sura's wider lesson? [* · links] (turns on: Whether the later recollection, Joseph's changed conduct, or the broader sura explains this scene.)
  12:42/q18/p1 The saved man's recollection in 12:45 confirms that he had forgotten Joseph. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi, al-Alusi, al-Tabataba'i and Kur'an Yolu use the later verse to support the cupbearer reading; al-Qurtubi adds that prophets may forget ordinary matters, while revelation is protected.
  12:42/q18/p2 Joseph's eventual refusal to answer the king immediately may repair his earlier appeal for royal help. — reasons: Al-Razi says Joseph put vindication of his name before favor from the king.
  12:42/q18/p3 The sura illustrates God's hidden direction of human affairs. — reasons: Asad contrasts Genesis' romantic account and cites 2:216: people may dislike what benefits them and like what harms them.
12:42/q19 Can prophets forget ordinary matters? [فَأَنسَىٰهُ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ · theology] (turns on: Whether the reported forgetting is ordinary and permissible or entails blameworthy satanic influence.)
  12:42/q19/p1 Yes; protection concerns conveying revelation, not every ordinary lapse. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites 12:45, 17:65 and hadith that Adam and the Prophet forgot; he uses this to answer an objection to the cupbearer reading.
  12:42/q19/p2 Joseph's sin

<<12:42 update 1, part 2 of 0..4>>
cerity and divine purification rule out blameworthy satanic access in this episode. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i rejects reports alleging grave lapses, while Ibn Kathir challenges their chains; Abu Hayyan says the stories should not be attributed to prophets.
12:42/q20 What inward reading is given to Joseph's request and continued imprisonment? [* · inward] (turns on: Which spiritual faculty or stage is represented by the forgotten messenger.)
  12:42/q20/p1 The request represents seeking stable spiritual existence through love, with a remnant of self that prolongs the journey. — reasons: Al-Qashani maps intoxicated love, spirit and heart toward unity, yet sees veiling rather than annihilation; ego or illusion can persist, and prison marks seclusion until subsistence through God begins.
  12:42/q20/p2 The alternative forgetting is the lover's loss of the love-messenger in bewildered witnessing. — reasons: Al-Qashani says unity makes the lover forget creation and self until annihilation ends and divine life restores distinction.
12:42/q21 What institutional lesson is drawn from Joseph's long imprisonment? [* · law]
  12:42/q21/p1 Prisons need regular judicial oversight so detainees do not disappear from official attention. — reasons: Ibn Ashur infers that the prison lacked a reliable register or periodic royal report, then says Islamic law requires a judge to review prisoners daily.
12:42/q22 What did Joseph's patience after imprisonment show? [* · reports]
  12:42/q22/p1 He interpreted the king's dream before asking for release and sought vindication before leaving prison. — reasons: Abd al-Razzaq transmits a Prophetic expression of admiration for his patience and generosity, while connecting the earlier request to longer confinement.
12:42/q23 How is the term of imprisonment connected to an earlier decree? [فَلَبِثَ فِى ٱلسِّجْنِ · links]
  12:42/q23/p1 The added years fulfill the earlier decision to imprison Joseph in 12:35. — reasons: Muqatil says the initial seven years and five later punitive years made twelve in all.
12:42/q24 What did Ali say about disciplining the soul in relation to this episode? [* · inward]
  12:42/q24/p1 The soul repeatedly scatters from discipline like a flock moving away from the shepherd. — reasons: Al-Tustari transmits Ali's comparison as an inward reflection on attention and self-discipline.
12:42/q25 Which prisoner was expected to survive? [ٱلَّذِى ظَنَّ أَنَّهُۥ نَاجٍۢ · referent]
  12:42/q25/p1 The surviving prisoner was the cupbearer. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi identifies him explicitly.
12:42/q26 Does a report of Joseph's request necessarily imply blame? [ٱذْكُرْنِى عِندَ رَبِّكَ · interpretation]
  12:42/q26/p1 Some scholars read Joseph's words without blame. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports this interpretive possibility, which accords with lawful use of means discussed elsewhere in the notes.
12:42/q27 How does al-Tabataba'i assess the al-Qummi account of the two prisoners? [* · reports]
  12:42/q27/p1 Its description of them as royal attendants assigned to guard Joseph is textually disordered. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says it conflicts with the Qur'an's description of them as Joseph's prison companions.

## THE NEW NOTES
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأممنقطعة)#515/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Disjunctive أم is not equivalent to أيهما: أعمرو عندك أم عندك زيد starts a fresh question after the first clause is complete.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأممنقطعة)#515/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Disconnected أم can follow a statement or a question when a new doubt arises after the first thought; إنها لإبل أم شاء is the declarative parallel.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأممنقطعة)#515/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Al-Khalil treats al-Akhtal's كذبتك عينك أم رأيت بواسط as the same disconnected أم construction as إنها لإبل أم شاء.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأممنقطعة)#515/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poetry may intend an interrogative and omit its initial hamza; examples are lines by al-Aswad al-Tamimi and ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabiʿa.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | لبث has the verbal noun لبثا, patterned like عمل عملا; the participle لابث confirms its membership in this class.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | وكالة, وصاية, and جراية follow ولاية because they mean taking charge; related terms include offices and forms of governance such as خلافة and سياسة.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Disease names need not use فعال; examples on other patterns are الحبط, الحبج, and الغدة.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | التجارة, الخياطة, and القصابة describe crafts and are modeled on وكالة; السعاية likewise names the work a person undertakes.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | فطنة follows the pattern of سرقة.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | رجحانا follows the pattern of الشكران and الرضوان.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Words with related meanings are often built alike: الصراف for the rutting of sheep is modeled on an agitated state, as are related forms such as الهباب and القراع.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابناءالأفعالالتيهيأعمالتعداكإلىغيركوتوقعهابهومصادرها#670/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | الهباب and القراع express agitation, and الضبعة is patterned like العوس.

[BAQILLANI:v1p277/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | A speaker’s character can show through imitation or artificial speech, revealing what he meant to conceal and making his words convey the opposite of his display.

[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p114/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Fronting the subject in affirmative reports strengthens promises and guarantees, where the listener may doubt fulfillment, and strengthens praise and boasting by forestalling doubt.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p114/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | When an action is expected and undisputed, Arabic normally reports it with the verb first, such as قد خرج or قد ركب, rather than foregrounding the subject.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p114/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | In circumstantial clauses, word order changes emphasis: subject-first wording makes a late arrival more reproachable, while saying someone came before sunrise more strongly marks haste.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p114/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The source says an unfronted construction with the sun not yet risen is awkward here; eloquent phrasing begins with the subject and builds the verb on it.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p119/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | أجاءك رجل asks whether any man came at all; it uses verb-first order because the question is about the occurrence of an arrival, not the visitor’s identity or kind.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p119/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | أرجل جاءك asks whether the already-known visitor was a man or a woman; putting the noun first asks about the agent’s kind.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p119/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | An indefinite noun cannot be fronted when neither an individual nor a known category is intended, because subject-first order asks about the agent’s identity or kind.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p119/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Modifiers can specify the category or identity being asked about: أرجل طويل asks tall or short, while a relative clause can distinguish a familiar giver from a stranger.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p119/r5] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | In a statement, رجل جاءني is apt only when correcting a belief about the visitor’s gender or category; otherwise the normal order is جاءني رجل.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p119/r6] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | In the proverb شر أهر ذا ناب, شر is fronted to identify the cause as evil rather than good, matching the sense of ما أهر ذا ناب إلا شر.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p119/r7] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Negation with إلا restricts an action to one known possibility and denies the rest; ما أتاني إلا رجل is appropriate only if the listener might think a woman came.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p256/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | إنما affirms an action for one person and denies that same action of another at once; جاءني زيد لا عمرو presents the two ideas in sequence.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p256/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A second advantage of إنما is that it makes the named person’s responsibility for the action more explicit than simple coordination with لا.

[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p257/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The correction assumes the listener knows that someone came but mistakenly attributes that arrival to Amr; the speaker identifies Zayd as the one who came.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p257/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Jurjani extends this analysis to إنما: it corrects who performed the mentioned action without implying that no one accompanied Zayd.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p93#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Quran's novel style overwhelmed even hostile rhetoricians, including converts Labid, Kab ibn Zuhayr, and al-Nabigha al-Jadi, as well as the stubborn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p93#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Because the Quran legislates, educates, and teaches, it appropriately places as many needed and rhetorically apt meanings as possible into concise wording, beyond ordinary eloquent speech.
